subject: Economics · Class 11 · Indian Economic Development
title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: an Appraisal
source: NCERT Class 11, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 3 (Reprint 2026-27)

reels.title: 1991: the turning point

scenes.text: There is a consensus in the world today that economic development is not all and the GDP is not necessarily a measure of progress of a society.
scenes.by: K.R. Narayanan, Former President of India
scenes.say: The chapter opens with former President K R Narayanan: There is a consensus in the world today that economic development is not all and the GDP is not necessarily a measure of progress of a society. G D P, gross domestic product, is the total value of the final goods and services a country produces in a year. Keep that line in mind as we judge the 1991 reforms.

scenes.heading: Was 1950–1990 a success? Two views

left.title: Critics
items: Rules and laws meant to control the economy
Ended up hampering growth and development

right.title: Supporters
items: Growth in savings
A diversified industrial sector
Expanding farm output and food security

scenes.say: Since independence, India ran a mixed economy. Some scholars argue that its many rules and laws, meant to control and regulate the economy, ended up hampering growth. Others say India, starting from near stagnation, grew its savings, built a diversified industrial sector and expanded farm output enough to ensure food security.

scenes.heading: 1991: the crisis

items.text: Couldn't repay borrowings from abroad (external debt)
Foreign exchange reserves not enough for even a fortnight of imports
Rising prices of essential goods

scenes.say: Then, in 1991, India hit an economic crisis over its external debt. The government couldn't repay what it had borrowed from abroad. Foreign exchange reserves, which India keeps to import petroleum and other important items, dropped so low they wouldn't last even a fortnight. And prices of essential goods were rising. This pushed the government into a new set of policies.

scenes.heading: This chapter
steps: Background of the crisis
The reforms: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation
Their impact on each sector
scenes.say: So this chapter covers three things: the background of the crisis, the reforms the government adopted, known as liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, and their impact on different sectors of the economy.

reels.beyond: The reforms were launched in July 1991 by Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's government, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 1 (why were reforms introduced?) starts here: the 1991 crisis in external debt, forex reserves and prices. 'LPG' is a staple of RBI Grade B ESI.

quiz.q: In 1991, India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to a level that was:
options: Not sufficient for even a fortnight of imports
Enough for about one year of imports
Enough for about six months of imports
Higher than ever before in India's history
quiz.why: NCERT: foreign exchange reserves dropped to levels that were not sufficient for even a fortnight.

cards.q: What three problems made up India's 1991 crisis (NCERT)?
cards.a: Inability to repay borrowings from abroad, forex reserves too low for even a fortnight of imports, and rising prices of essential goods.

cards.q: Who said GDP is 'not necessarily a measure of progress of a society'?
cards.a: K.R. Narayanan, former President of India (the chapter's opening quote).

reels.title: Concept: balance of payments & forex reserves

scenes.heading: Why India needs dollars

items.text: Imports like petroleum are paid for in dollars
We earn those dollars from our exports
Foreign exchange reserves: the stock of foreign currency kept for imports

scenes.say: Start with a simple fact from NCERT. When India imports goods like petroleum, it pays in dollars, and it earns those dollars from its exports. The foreign currency the country keeps aside, mainly to pay for imports like petroleum, is its foreign exchange reserves.

scenes.heading: Balance of payments, defined

items.text: A record of all transactions between a country and the rest of the world in a period
Money coming in: exports, remittances, foreign investment, loans
Money going out: imports, interest, loan repayments

scenes.say: NCERT uses the term balance of payments without defining it, so here's the standard definition, beyond the book. The balance of payments, or B o P, is a record of all money transactions between a country and the rest of the world in a period. Money coming in: exports, remittances, foreign investment and loans. Money going out: imports, interest and loan repayments.

scenes.heading: Think of a household

left.title: A family
items: Salary coming in
Bills and EMIs going out
Savings account as a cushion

right.title: A country
items: Exports and inflows
Imports and debt payments
Forex reserves as a cushion

scenes.say: An analogy. A family has salary coming in and bills and loan payments going out, with a savings account as a cushion. A country has exports and inflows coming in, imports and debt payments going out, and forex reserves as its cushion. When outflows keep beating inflows, the cushion drains. That's a balance of payments crisis.

That is exactly what happened in 1991. Outflows had exceeded inflows for years, and the reserves cushion was nearly empty. NCERT's Unit introduction puts it plainly: a crisis in the balance of payments led to the economic reforms.

reels.beyond: The balance of payments has two main parts. The current account covers trade in goods and services, plus income and transfers. The capital account covers investment and loans. RBI publishes India's BoP data every quarter.
reels.examAngle: Balance of payments is core RBI Grade B material (Phase 1 GA and Phase 2 ESI/Finance). Be able to explain it in one line and link it to 1991.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, India pays for imports like petroleum mainly with:
options: Dollars earned from its exports
Rupees printed by the RBI for trade
Gold borrowed from the World Bank
Taxes collected from importers
quiz.why: NCERT: when we import goods like petroleum, we pay in dollars, which we earn from our exports.

cards.q: What are foreign exchange reserves, and what does India keep them for?
cards.a: The stock of foreign currency a country holds; India keeps them mainly to import petroleum and other important items.

cards.q: Define balance of payments (standard definition, beyond NCERT).
cards.a: A record of all transactions between a country and the rest of the world in a period: inflows (exports, investment, loans) and outflows (imports, interest, repayments).

cards.q: What kind of crisis triggered the 1991 reforms?
cards.a: A balance of payments crisis: foreign exchange reserves had nearly run out.

reels.title: Concept: the government's deficit

scenes.heading: How the government is funded
steps: Income: taxes and public sector enterprises
Expenditure: policies and administration
Spending more than income = a deficit
The deficit is covered by borrowing
scenes.say: To run its policies and administration, NCERT says, the government raises money from sources like taxation and running public sector enterprises. When its expenditure is more than its income, the gap is called a deficit, and the government borrows to cover it.

scenes.heading: Who the government borrows from

items.text: Banks
People within the country
International financial institutions

scenes.say: It borrows from banks, from people within the country, and from international financial institutions. Borrowing isn't wrong in itself. The trouble starts when it keeps growing faster than the government's ability to repay.

scenes.heading: Fiscal deficit

items.text: Total expenditure minus total receipts, not counting borrowing
Usually quoted as a percentage of GDP
Like a household that keeps funding its bills on credit
Indian example: Budget 2025-26 target, 4.4% of GDP

scenes.say: Beyond the book, the key measure is the fiscal deficit: the government's total expenditure minus its total receipts, not counting borrowings. In other words, how much it must borrow in a year. It's usually quoted as a percentage of G D P. Think of a household that keeps paying its bills on a credit card: fine for a while, dangerous if it never stops. A real Indian example: the Union Budget for 2025-26 set a fiscal deficit target of 4.4 percent of G D P.

reels.beyond: India's FRBM Act (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003) set rules to bring the fiscal deficit down. The Union Budget states each year's fiscal deficit target.
reels.examAngle: Fiscal deficit is one of the most-asked RBI Grade B terms. Know the definition, and link the 1980s deficits to the 1991 crisis.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, when the government's expenditure is more than its income, it:
options: Borrows to finance the deficit
Must close down public enterprises
Stops all development spending
Asks the RBI to fix interest rates
quiz.why: NCERT: when expenditure is more than income, the government borrows to finance the deficit from banks, people and international financial institutions.

cards.q: Which two sources of government income does NCERT give as examples?
cards.a: Taxation and running public sector enterprises.

cards.q: From whom does the government borrow to finance a deficit (NCERT)?
cards.a: Banks, people within the country, and international financial institutions.

cards.q: Define fiscal deficit (beyond NCERT).
cards.a: Total government expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings, i.e. what it must borrow in a year.

reels.title: How the crisis built up in the 1980s

scenes.big: The crisis was built over a decade.
scenes.sub: Inefficient management of the economy in the 1980s
scenes.say: NCERT traces the origin of the financial crisis to the inefficient management of the Indian economy in the 1980s. It didn't happen overnight. Let's see how it built up, brick by brick.

scenes.heading: Spending without matching revenue

items.text: Spent beyond revenue to fight unemployment, poverty and population growth
Big shares went to areas with no immediate returns: social sector, defence
Public sector undertakings didn't earn enough
Not enough raised from taxation

scenes.say: Even though revenues were very low, development policies needed the government to overshoot its revenue to tackle unemployment, poverty and population growth. That spending didn't generate extra revenue. Large shares went to areas without immediate returns, like the social sector and defence. Income from public sector undertakings wasn't high, and the government couldn't raise enough through taxation.

scenes.heading: And on the foreign side

items.text: Borrowed foreign exchange was spent on consumption
No attempt to cut 'profligate' (wasteful) spending
Too little attention to boosting exports

scenes.say: At times, foreign exchange borrowed from other countries and international institutions was spent on meeting consumption needs, not on things that would earn it back. There was no attempt to reduce such profligate, meaning wasteful, spending, and not enough attention to boosting exports to pay for the growing imports.

reels.beyond: Economists often describe the 1980s as growth fuelled by borrowing, with both a large fiscal deficit and a large current account deficit. They call these the 'twin deficits'.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 1 asks why reforms were introduced. List these causes before the 1991 trigger: overspending without revenue, low PSU income, forex used for consumption, and neglect of exports.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, how was borrowed foreign exchange sometimes used in the 1980s?
options: To meet consumption needs
To build new export industries
To repay all past foreign loans
To build up gold reserves
quiz.why: NCERT: at times, foreign exchange borrowed from other countries and international financial institutions was spent on meeting consumption needs.

cards.q: What does NCERT say was the origin of the 1991 financial crisis?
cards.a: Inefficient management of the Indian economy in the 1980s.

cards.q: Name the 1980s mistakes that NCERT says led to the crisis.
cards.a: Spending beyond revenue, big spending without immediate returns (social sector, defence), low PSU income, borrowed forex used for consumption; no curb on wasteful spending or push for exports.

reels.title: Two weeks of reserves: the 1991 crisis

scenes.heading: The late 1980s spiral
steps: Expenditure far exceeds revenue
Borrowing becomes unsustainable
Prices of essential goods rise; imports outrun exports
Reserves cover barely two weeks of imports
scenes.say: In the late 1980s, government expenditure exceeded revenue by such large margins that borrowing to cover it became unsustainable. Prices of many essential goods rose sharply. Imports grew very fast without matching exports. Reserves fell to a level not enough to finance imports for more than two weeks.

scenes.heading: No one would lend

items.text: Not enough foreign exchange even to pay interest to international lenders
No country or international funder willing to lend to India

scenes.say: There wasn't even enough foreign exchange to pay the interest owed to international lenders. And no country or international funder was willing to lend to India.

scenes.heading: The rescue
steps: India approaches the World Bank (IBRD) and the IMF
Receives $7 billion as a loan
Conditions: liberalise and open up
India agrees: New Economic Policy (NEP)
scenes.say: India approached the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, popularly called the World Bank, and the International Monetary Fund, the I M F. It received 7 billion dollars as a loan. In return, they expected India to liberalise and open up the economy. India agreed, and announced the New Economic Policy, or N E P.

scenes.heading: The conditionalities

items.text: Remove restrictions on the private sector
Reduce the role of the government in many areas
Remove trade restrictions between India and other countries

scenes.say: The conditions were: remove restrictions on the private sector, reduce the role of the government in many areas, and remove trade restrictions between India and other countries.

reels.beyond: Beyond the book: the IMF lends to countries facing balance of payments trouble; the World Bank lends for long-term development projects; both were set up in 1944. To raise emergency loans in 1991, India also pledged part of its gold reserves abroad, a moment often cited as the low point of the crisis.
reels.examAngle: NCERT's own wording is useful in exams: reserves 'not sufficient for even a fortnight' (3.1) and 'not adequate to finance imports for more than two weeks' (3.2). They mean the same thing. Remember the $7 billion loan, and that the World Bank's formal name is the IBRD.

quiz.q: How much did India receive as a loan from the World Bank and IMF in 1991, according to NCERT?
options: $7 billion
$70 billion
$700 million
$17 billion
quiz.why: NCERT: India approached the IBRD (World Bank) and the IMF and received $7 billion as loan to manage the crisis.

cards.q: What is the formal name of the World Bank (as given by NCERT)?
cards.a: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD).

cards.q: What conditions came with the 1991 World Bank and IMF loan?
cards.a: Liberalise and open up: remove restrictions on the private sector, reduce the government's role, remove trade restrictions.

cards.q: What loan did India get in 1991 and what policy followed?
cards.a: $7 billion from the World Bank and IMF; India agreed to their conditions and announced the New Economic Policy (NEP).

cards.q: IMF vs World Bank, in one line each (beyond NCERT)?
cards.a: IMF: lends to countries facing balance of payments trouble. World Bank: lends for long-term development projects. Both set up in 1944.

reels.title: The NEP: stabilisation vs structural reform

scenes.heading: The thrust of the NEP

items.text: A more competitive environment in the economy
Remove barriers to entry and growth of firms

scenes.say: The New Economic Policy was a wide-ranging set of reforms. Its thrust, NCERT says, was creating a more competitive environment in the economy, and removing the barriers to entry and growth of firms.

scenes.heading: Inflation, in one line

items.text: Inflation: a sustained rise in the general level of prices
Same ₹100 buys less than before

scenes.say: First, one term, beyond the book. Inflation is a sustained rise in the general level of prices, so the same hundred rupees buys less than before. Controlling it is one of the RBI's main jobs.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of measures

left.title: Stabilisation (short-term)
items: Correct weaknesses in the balance of payments
Bring inflation under control
Keep enough forex; keep prices in check

right.title: Structural reform (long-term)
items: Improve the economy's efficiency
Raise international competitiveness
Remove rigidities across sectors

scenes.say: The policies fall into two groups. Stabilisation measures are short-term: they correct weaknesses in the balance of payments and bring inflation under control. Simply put, keep enough foreign exchange reserves and keep rising prices in check. Structural reforms are long-term: they improve the economy's efficiency and international competitiveness by removing rigidities in various sectors.

scenes.heading: An analogy

left.title: Stabilisation = emergency care
items: Stop the bleeding now
1991: rebuild forex reserves, bring inflation down

right.title: Structural reform = lifestyle change
items: Get fit so the illness doesn't return
1991: abolish industrial licensing, cut tariffs

scenes.say: An analogy, beyond the book. Stabilisation is like emergency treatment for a patient: stop the bleeding now. In 1991, that meant rebuilding foreign exchange reserves and bringing inflation down. Structural reform is like changing the patient's lifestyle so the illness doesn't return: abolishing industrial licensing and cutting tariffs, so the economy becomes efficient for the long run.

scenes.heading: Three heads of reform
steps: Liberalisation
Privatisation
Globalisation
scenes.say: The government's policies fall under three heads: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, often called L P G. The next reels take them one by one.

reels.beyond: India's inflation target, under the flexible inflation-targeting framework adopted in 2016, is 4% consumer price inflation, with a band of 2 to 6%. RBI's Monetary Policy Committee works to it.
reels.examAngle: A classic short answer: distinguish stabilisation (short-term: BoP, inflation) from structural reform (long-term: efficiency, competitiveness). Then name the three heads: L, P, G.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, stabilisation measures under the NEP were:
options: Short-term, to correct the balance of payments and control inflation
Long-term, to improve efficiency and international competitiveness
Short-term, to sell public sector companies to private firms
Long-term, to raise taxes on all imported goods
quiz.why: Stabilisation: short-term (BoP weaknesses, inflation). Structural reforms: long-term (efficiency, competitiveness, removing rigidities).

cards.q: Stabilisation vs structural reform measures?
cards.a: Stabilisation: short-term, correct balance of payments weaknesses and control inflation. Structural: long-term, improve efficiency and international competitiveness by removing rigidities.

cards.q: What was the thrust of the New Economic Policy (NCERT)?
cards.a: A more competitive environment and removing barriers to entry and growth of firms.

cards.q: Define inflation (beyond NCERT).
cards.a: A sustained rise in the general level of prices.

cards.q: Give one 1991 example each of a stabilisation and a structural measure.
cards.a: Stabilisation: rebuilding forex reserves and controlling inflation. Structural: abolishing industrial licensing, cutting tariffs.

reels.title: Liberalisation 1: freeing industry

scenes.heading: Liberalisation: ending the controls

items.text: A few steps in the 1980s: licensing, export-import policy, technology, fiscal policy, foreign investment
1991 reforms: far more comprehensive

scenes.say: Liberalisation means ending the restrictions that had become hindrances to growth, and opening up sectors of the economy. A few liberalisation measures came in the 1980s, in industrial licensing, export-import policy, technology upgradation, fiscal policy and foreign investment. But the 1991 reforms were far more comprehensive.

scenes.heading: The old controls on industry

items.text: Licence needed to start a firm, close it, or decide output
Private sector barred from many industries
Some goods only by small-scale industries
Controls on price fixation and distribution

scenes.say: Before 1991, industry was controlled in four ways. Industrial licensing: every entrepreneur needed government permission to start a firm, close it, or decide how much to produce. The private sector wasn't allowed in many industries. Some goods could only be made by small-scale industries. And there were controls on fixing prices and distributing selected products.

scenes.heading: After 1991

items.text: Licensing abolished for almost all, except alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace, drugs and pharmaceuticals
Reserved for the public sector: part of atomic energy, some core railway activities
Many small-scale goods dereserved
Markets now set prices in most industries

scenes.say: The reforms removed many of these. Industrial licensing was abolished for almost all products except alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace, and drugs and pharmaceuticals. The only industries still reserved for the public sector are a part of atomic energy generation and some core activities in railway transport. Many goods made by small-scale industries were dereserved. And in most industries, the market now sets prices.

reels.beyond: Compare with Chapter 2: IPR 1956 reserved 17 industries for the state (Schedule A). After 1991, almost all of that list was opened up.
reels.examAngle: MCQ favourites: which industries still need a licence, and the only two areas still reserved for the public sector (part of atomic energy generation, and core railway transport activities).

quiz.q: According to NCERT, which industries are still reserved for the public sector after the reforms?
options: A part of atomic energy generation and some core railway activities
Banking, insurance, telecommunications and the whole of civil aviation
Iron and steel, cement, fertilisers and heavy electrical machinery
Coal mining, oil refining, ports and all defence equipment production
quiz.why: NCERT: the only industries now reserved for the public sector are a part of atomic energy generation and some core activities in railway transport.

cards.q: For which products is an industrial licence still required (NCERT)?
cards.a: Alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace, and drugs and pharmaceuticals.

cards.q: What were the four kinds of industrial controls before 1991?
cards.a: Industrial licensing (start, close, output), private sector barred from many industries, some goods only by SSIs, controls on prices and distribution.

cards.q: What does 'dereserved' mean in the reforms?
cards.a: Goods once reserved for small-scale industries were opened to other producers.

reels.title: Liberalisation 2: the financial sector and RBI

scenes.heading: What is the financial sector?

items.text: Commercial banks and investment banks
Stock exchange operations
The foreign exchange market

scenes.say: The financial sector includes financial institutions such as commercial banks and investment banks, stock exchange operations, and the foreign exchange market. In India it's regulated by the Reserve Bank of India, the R B I.

scenes.heading: How RBI controls banks (NCERT)

items.text: Decides how much money banks can keep with themselves
Fixes interest rates
Decides the nature of lending to various sectors

scenes.say: All banks follow R B I's norms and regulations. The R B I decides the amount of money banks can keep with themselves, fixes interest rates, and decides the nature of lending to various sectors. A major aim of the reforms was to change R B I's role from regulator to facilitator, letting the financial sector decide many matters without consulting the R B I.

scenes.heading: What changed

items.text: Private sector banks, Indian and foreign, allowed
Foreign investment limit in banks raised to about 74%
Qualifying banks can open branches and rationalise existing ones without RBI approval
Managerial aspects stay with RBI to protect account-holders
Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) can invest in Indian markets

scenes.say: The reforms allowed private sector banks, Indian and foreign. Foreign investment in banks was raised to around 74 percent. Banks meeting certain conditions can set up new branches and rationalise existing ones without R B I approval. But R B I kept certain managerial aspects to protect account-holders and the nation. And Foreign Institutional Investors, or F I Is, such as merchant bankers, mutual funds and pension funds, can now invest in Indian financial markets.

reels.beyond: The RBI controls how much money banks keep through tools like the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR, a share of deposits kept with RBI) and the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR, a share kept in safe assets like government securities). Both are core RBI Grade B topics.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 3 (the exercise says 'controller', the text says 'regulator'): rules and controls had become hindrances to growth, so the reforms let the financial sector take decisions on many matters without consulting the RBI; private and foreign banks entered and FIIs could invest, while the RBI kept managerial aspects to protect account-holders. Exercise 4: the RBI controls banks by deciding the money they keep with themselves, fixing interest rates and deciding the nature of lending.

quiz.q: A major aim of financial sector reforms, according to NCERT, was to change RBI's role from:
options: Regulator to facilitator
Facilitator to regulator
Lender to borrower
Banker to tax collector
quiz.why: NCERT: one of the major aims of financial sector reforms is to reduce the role of RBI from regulator to facilitator of the financial sector.

cards.q: How does the RBI control commercial banks (NCERT, Exercise 4)?
cards.a: It decides how much money banks can keep with themselves, fixes interest rates, and decides the nature of lending to various sectors.

cards.q: What was the foreign investment limit in banks raised to?
cards.a: Around 74 per cent.

cards.q: Give three examples of Foreign Institutional Investors (NCERT).
cards.a: Merchant bankers, mutual funds and pension funds.

cards.q: Why did the RBI's role change from regulator (Exercise 3 says 'controller') to facilitator?
cards.a: To remove controls that hampered growth: the financial sector could decide many matters without consulting the RBI. The RBI kept managerial aspects to protect account-holders.

reels.title: Liberalisation 3: tax reforms and GST

scenes.heading: Fiscal policy: two kinds of tax

left.title: Direct taxes
items: On incomes of individuals
On profits of businesses
e.g. income tax, corporation tax

right.title: Indirect taxes
items: Levied on goods and services
e.g. GST (NCERT), customs duty

scenes.say: The government's taxation and public expenditure policies together are called its fiscal policy. There are two types of taxes. Direct taxes are on the incomes of individuals and the profits of businesses, like income tax and corporation tax. Indirect taxes are levied on goods and services. Examples are G S T, which NCERT discusses next, and, beyond the book, customs duty.

scenes.heading: Why lower income tax?
steps: High income tax rates caused tax evasion
Rates cut continuously since 1991
Moderate rates encourage savings and honest disclosure
Corporation tax also gradually reduced
scenes.say: Since 1991, taxes on individual incomes have been cut continuously, because high income tax rates were seen as a major reason for tax evasion. It's now widely accepted that moderate rates encourage savings and voluntary disclosure of income. The once very high corporation tax was also gradually reduced.

scenes.heading: GST: one nation, one tax

items.text: 2016: Constitution amended so the Union and states can levy GST
Expected to raise revenue and reduce tax evasion
'One nation, one tax and one market'

scenes.say: Indirect taxes were reformed to create a common national market. In 2016, the Constitution was amended so that both the Union government and the states could levy the Goods and Services Tax, or G S T. It's expected to raise revenue, reduce tax evasion and create one nation, one tax and one market.

scenes.heading: What GST changed

items.text: Before: central excise, service tax, state VAT, entry tax and more, varying by state
From 1 July 2017: one tax on the supply of goods and services, shared by Centre and states
Like one toll pass for the whole country instead of a booth at every state border

scenes.say: Beyond the book: what G S T actually changed. Before it, a product could be taxed many times over, through central excise, service tax, and state VAT and entry taxes that differed from state to state. G S T, in force since 1 July 2017, replaced many of these with a single tax on the supply of goods and services, shared by the Centre and the states. Think of one toll pass for the whole country instead of a toll booth at every state border.

scenes.heading: Tax reform in general: simplification

items.text: Many procedures simplified
Rates substantially lowered
Aim: better compliance by taxpayers

scenes.say: Separately, NCERT notes another component of tax reform: simplification. To encourage better compliance by taxpayers, many procedures were simplified and rates substantially lowered.

reels.beyond: The 2016 amendment was the 101st Constitutional Amendment, and GST came into force on 1 July 2017. It replaced many central and state indirect taxes.
reels.examAngle: Know NCERT's definition of fiscal policy, the direct vs indirect difference, why rates were cut (evasion, savings, disclosure), and GST's slogan.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, why were income tax rates cut after 1991?
options: High rates were a major reason for tax evasion
The IMF banned income tax in India
Income tax was replaced entirely by GST
Indirect taxes had been abolished
quiz.why: NCERT: it was felt that high rates of income tax were an important reason for tax evasion; moderate rates encourage savings and voluntary disclosure.

cards.q: Define fiscal policy (NCERT).
cards.a: The government's taxation and public expenditure policies, taken together.

cards.q: Direct vs indirect taxes?
cards.a: Direct: on incomes of individuals and profits of businesses (income tax, corporation tax). Indirect: levied on goods and services (e.g. GST).

cards.q: What did the 2016 constitutional amendment enable, and what is GST's slogan?
cards.a: The Union and states could levy the Goods and Services Tax; 'one nation, one tax and one market'.

cards.q: What is GST and when did it start (beyond NCERT)?
cards.a: A single indirect tax on the supply of goods and services, shared by Centre and states, replacing many earlier taxes; in force from 1 July 2017.

reels.title: Concept: devaluation and exchange rates

scenes.heading: Foreign exchange reform, 1991

items.text: The rupee was devalued against foreign currencies
This increased the inflow of foreign exchange
Set the tone for freeing the rupee's value from government control

scenes.say: The first important external reform was in the foreign exchange market. In 1991, as an immediate step to resolve the balance of payments crisis, the rupee was devalued against foreign currencies. This increased the inflow of foreign exchange, and set the tone for freeing the rupee's value from government control.

scenes.heading: Devaluation, with an example

left.title: Before
items: A $10 Indian shirt costs ₹200 to make
Imported $100 machine costs ₹2,000

right.title: After devaluation
items: Same ₹200 shirt now sells for $8: cheaper abroad
Same machine now costs ₹2,500: dearer at home

scenes.say: Beyond the book: devaluation means the government lowers the rupee's official value, so each dollar buys more rupees. Say a dollar goes from 20 to 25 rupees. An Indian shirt costing 200 rupees now sells abroad for 8 dollars instead of 10, so exports get cheaper and sell more. But an imported 100-dollar machine now costs 2,500 rupees instead of 2,000, so imports get dearer. An everyday picture: it's like a sale on everything Indian for foreign buyers, and a price hike on everything foreign for Indian buyers.

scenes.heading: Today: the market decides

items.text: Exchange rates set by the demand and supply of foreign exchange
More often than not, markets, not the government

scenes.say: Now, more often than not, NCERT says, markets determine exchange rates, based on the demand and supply of foreign exchange. If more people want dollars than are on offer, the dollar gets dearer in rupees, and the other way round.

reels.beyond: In July 1991, the rupee was devalued in two steps, about 18 to 19 percent in total. Devaluation means a government lowering a fixed rate. Depreciation means a market-driven fall, which is how the rupee usually moves today.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 5: what is devaluation of the rupee? Define it, say why India did it in 1991 (BoP crisis; boost forex inflow), and note that markets now set the rate.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, devaluing the rupee in 1991 led to:
options: An increase in the inflow of foreign exchange
A sharp fall in India's exports
Fixed exchange rates set by the RBI
Cheaper imports of petroleum
quiz.why: NCERT: the rupee was devalued against foreign currencies, which led to an increase in the inflow of foreign exchange.

cards.q: What is devaluation of the rupee?
cards.a: Lowering the rupee's official value against foreign currencies, so a dollar buys more rupees: exports get cheaper abroad, imports dearer.

cards.q: Why did India devalue the rupee in 1991 (NCERT)?
cards.a: As an immediate measure to resolve the balance of payments crisis; it increased the inflow of foreign exchange.

cards.q: How are exchange rates determined now (NCERT)?
cards.a: More often than not, by the market, based on the demand and supply of foreign exchange.

reels.title: Liberalisation 4: opening trade

scenes.heading: Two old shields, defined

left.title: Tariff
items: A tax on imported goods
Makes imports dearer

right.title: Quantitative restriction (QR)
items: A limit on how much can be imported or exported
e.g. a quota

scenes.say: To protect domestic industry, India kept a regime of quantitative restrictions on imports, with tight control over imports and very high tariffs. NCERT says these policies reduced efficiency and competitiveness, slowing manufacturing growth. In plain terms, beyond the book: a tariff is a tax on imported goods, and a quantitative restriction, or Q R, is a limit on the quantity that can be imported or exported, like a quota.

scenes.heading: Tariff vs quota, in a picture

left.title: Tariff = an entry fee
items: Anyone can come in, at a price
Works through price

right.title: Quota = a guest list
items: Only a fixed number get in
Works through quantity

scenes.say: An analogy, beyond the book. A tariff is like an entry fee at a gate: anyone can come in, but it costs more. A quota is like a guest list: only a fixed number get in, however much they'd pay. NCERT gives a quota example later: the U S A's quotas on textile imports from India and China. Beyond the book, those textile quotas ended in 2005.

scenes.heading: The trade reforms aimed at

items.text: Dismantling quantitative restrictions on imports and exports
Reducing tariff rates
Removing licensing procedures for imports

scenes.say: Trade and investment reforms aimed to raise the international competitiveness of industry, bring in foreign investment and technology, and promote efficiency. They had three parts: dismantling quantitative restrictions on imports and exports, reducing tariff rates, and removing licensing procedures for imports.

scenes.heading: Key results

items.text: Import licensing abolished, except hazardous and environmentally sensitive industries
From April 2001: QRs on manufactured consumer goods and farm products fully removed
Export duties removed, to help Indian goods compete abroad

scenes.say: Import licensing was abolished, except for hazardous and environmentally sensitive industries. From April 2001, quantitative restrictions on imports of manufactured consumer goods and agricultural products were fully removed. And export duties were removed, to make Indian goods more competitive in international markets.

reels.beyond: Removing QRs by April 2001 was one of India's WTO commitments. Today India protects trade mainly through tariffs, with some anti-dumping duties.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 7 (why are tariffs imposed? To protect domestic industry by making imports dearer) and Exercise 8 (meaning of quantitative restrictions: limits on the quantity of imports or exports).

quiz.q: From when were quantitative restrictions on imports of manufactured consumer goods and agricultural products fully removed?
options: April 2001
July 1991
January 1995
April 2016
quiz.why: NCERT: quantitative restrictions on imports of manufactured consumer goods and agricultural products were fully removed from April 2001.

cards.q: What are quantitative restrictions (Exercise 8)?
cards.a: Limits on the quantity of goods that can be imported or exported (e.g. quotas).

cards.q: What were the three aims of the trade reforms (NCERT)?
cards.a: Dismantle quantitative restrictions on imports and exports, reduce tariff rates, remove licensing procedures for imports.

cards.q: Why were export duties removed?
cards.a: To increase the competitive position of Indian goods in international markets.

cards.q: Tariff vs quota?
cards.a: Tariff: a tax that makes imports dearer (works through price). Quota: a fixed limit on the quantity allowed in.

reels.title: Privatisation and disinvestment

scenes.heading: Privatisation: two routes

items.text: Government withdraws from ownership and management of public sector companies
Outright sale of public sector companies

scenes.say: Privatisation means shedding the ownership or management of a government-owned enterprise. NCERT gives two routes: the government withdraws from ownership and management of public sector companies, or it sells them outright.

scenes.heading: Disinvestment

items.text: Selling part of the equity (shares) of public sector enterprises (PSEs) to the public
Aim: financial discipline and modernisation
Use private capital and managerial skills
Privatisation was expected to attract foreign direct investment (FDI)

scenes.say: Privatising public sector enterprises, or P S Es, by selling part of their equity, meaning shares, to the public is called disinvestment. The government's stated purpose was mainly to improve financial discipline and help modernisation, using private capital and managerial skills to improve the P S Us. It also hoped privatisation would give a strong push to foreign direct investment, or F D I: foreigners building or buying into businesses in India for the long term.

scenes.heading: Disinvestment, made concrete

items.text: Like a family selling a few shares of its shop to neighbours, but still running it
Example: LIC's IPO, May 2022: about 3.5% of the government's stake sold to the public

scenes.say: An analogy, beyond the book. A family sells a few shares of its shop to neighbours: it raises cash, but still runs the shop. A real Indian example: in May 2022, the government sold about 3.5 percent of its stake in L I C, the Life Insurance Corporation, to the public, and kept control.

scenes.heading: Strategic vs minority sale

left.title: Strategic sale
items: Sells a large stake
Management control passes to the buyer
e.g. Air India sold to the Tata group (2022)

right.title: Minority sale
items: Sells less than half the shares
Government keeps control

scenes.say: Exercise 6 asks you to distinguish a strategic sale from a minority sale, which NCERT doesn't explain, so this is beyond the book. In a strategic sale, the government sells a large stake and management control passes to the buyer. Air India, sold to the Tata group in 2022, is an example. In a minority sale, the government sells less than half the shares, often to the public, and keeps control.

reels.beyond: Disinvestment is handled by DIPAM, the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management in the Ministry of Finance. NCERT lists its website among the chapter's references.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 6(i), strategic vs minority sale, needs the beyond-the-book definitions. Also know NCERT's two routes to privatisation, and its definition of disinvestment.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, 'disinvestment' means:
options: Selling part of the equity of public sector enterprises to the public
Government buying shares of loss-making private companies
Closing down every public sector enterprise
Stopping all foreign investment in Indian firms
quiz.why: NCERT: privatisation of PSEs by selling off part of their equity to the public is known as disinvestment.

cards.q: What are the two routes to privatisation (NCERT)?
cards.a: Government withdrawal from ownership and management of public sector companies, or their outright sale.

cards.q: Define disinvestment and its stated purpose.
cards.a: Selling part of PSEs' equity to the public; purpose: improve financial discipline and facilitate modernisation using private capital and management. Example (beyond NCERT): LIC's 2022 IPO, about 3.5% of the government's stake.

cards.q: Strategic sale vs minority sale (beyond NCERT)?
cards.a: Strategic: a large stake with management control to the buyer (e.g. Air India to Tatas). Minority: under half the shares, government keeps control.

reels.title: Maharatnas, Navratnas, Miniratnas

scenes.big: Nine jewels of a royal court, now public companies.
scenes.sub: Box 3.1: Navratnas and public enterprise policies
scenes.say: The name comes from the famous Navratnas, the nine jewels of King Vikramaditya's court: eminent people in art, literature and knowledge. Since the reforms, the government has given top public sector enterprises special jewel-like status.

scenes.heading: Why the status?

items.text: Improve efficiency, infuse professionalism
Compete better in a liberalised global market
More financial, managerial and operational autonomy

scenes.say: To improve efficiency, bring in professionalism and help them compete in the liberalised global environment, the government declares certain public sector enterprises as maharatnas, navratnas and miniratnas. They get greater financial, managerial and operational autonomy in their decisions, so they can run efficiently and increase profits.

scenes.heading: NCERT's examples

items.text: Maharatnas: Indian Oil Corporation, Steel Authority of India
Navratnas: Hindustan Aeronautics, Mahanagar Telephone Nigam, IRCTC
Miniratnas: Bharat Sanchar Nigam, Airports Authority of India

scenes.say: NCERT's examples. Maharatnas: Indian Oil Corporation and Steel Authority of India. Navratnas: Hindustan Aeronautics, Mahanagar Telephone Nigam, and the Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation, I R C T C. Miniratnas: Bharat Sanchar Nigam and the Airports Authority of India.

scenes.heading: The debate

left.title: Result
items: Many were set up in the 1950s–60s for self-reliance
Status improved these companies' performance

right.title: Criticism and update
items: Scholars: partly privatised through disinvestment instead
Later: government chose to keep them public and let them grow globally

scenes.say: Many of these profitable companies were set up in the 1950s and 60s, when self-reliance mattered, to build infrastructure and provide jobs. Granting the status improved their performance. Scholars allege that instead of helping them grow, the government partly privatised them through disinvestment. More recently, it has decided to keep them in the public sector and let them expand in global markets.

reels.beyond: These statuses change over time. Hindustan Aeronautics, listed by NCERT as a Navratna, was upgraded to Maharatna in 2024. Use NCERT's list for NCERT questions, and current lists for current-affairs questions.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 12: does the navratna policy improve PSU performance? Yes, through autonomy and professionalism, but note the critics' point about disinvestment. Expect MCQs matching companies to their category.

quiz.q: Which pair is correctly matched as per NCERT's Box 3.1?
options: Maharatna: Steel Authority of India
Miniratna: Indian Oil Corporation
Navratna: Airports Authority of India
Maharatna: Bharat Sanchar Nigam
quiz.why: NCERT: Maharatnas – IOC, SAIL; Navratnas – HAL, MTNL, IRCTC; Miniratnas – BSNL, Airports Authority of India.

cards.q: What does Maharatna/Navratna/Miniratna status give a public sector enterprise?
cards.a: Greater financial, managerial and operational autonomy, to improve efficiency and compete globally.

cards.q: NCERT's examples of Maharatnas, Navratnas and Miniratnas?
cards.a: Maharatnas: IOC, SAIL. Navratnas: HAL, MTNL, IRCTC. Miniratnas: BSNL, Airports Authority of India.

cards.q: Where does the name 'Navratna' come from (NCERT)?
cards.a: The nine jewels (Navratnas) of King Vikramaditya's court: eminent people in art, literature and knowledge.

reels.title: Globalisation and outsourcing

scenes.heading: Globalisation

items.text: Integration of the country's economy with the world economy
Networks across economic, social and geographical boundaries
Events miles away affect India: a 'borderless world'
Recap: the outcome of liberalisation and privatisation

scenes.say: Globalisation is generally understood as integrating a country's economy with the world economy. But NCERT calls it a complex phenomenon: it creates networks and activities that cross economic, social and geographical boundaries, so that events miles away can influence what happens in India. It's turning the world into one whole, a borderless world. NCERT's text calls it the outcome of a set of policies aimed at greater interdependence and integration of the world; the Recap puts it simply: the outcome of the policies of liberalisation and privatisation.

scenes.heading: Outsourcing
steps: A company used to do a service in-house
Now it hires it from an outside provider
Often in another country
Fast communication and IT make it possible
scenes.say: Outsourcing is one important outcome. A company hires a regular service from an outside source, mostly from other countries, that was earlier provided internally, like legal advice, computer services, advertising or security. It has grown because of fast communication, especially information technology. NCERT's Recap calls outsourcing a major emerging activity in both industry and services.

scenes.heading: What gets outsourced to India

items.text: Voice-based business processes: BPOs and call centres
Record keeping, accountancy, banking services
Music recording, film editing, book transcription
Clinical advice, even teaching

scenes.say: Many services are outsourced to India: voice-based business processes, known as B P Os or call centres, record keeping, accountancy, banking services, music recording, film editing, book transcription, clinical advice, and even teaching. With the internet, text, voice and visual data can be sent across continents in real time.

scenes.heading: Why India?

items.text: Low wage rates
Available skilled manpower

scenes.say: Why India? NCERT gives two reasons: low wage rates and the availability of skilled manpower. So companies can get the work done at lower cost, with a reasonable degree of skill and accuracy. That has made India a destination for global outsourcing since the reforms.

reels.beyond: Developed countries often oppose outsourcing because it moves jobs away from their own workers. This is the second half of NCERT's Exercise 10.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 10: largely yes: outsourcing creates jobs (NCERT's Fig. 3.1 calls it 'a new employment opportunity in big cities'), brings in foreign exchange (Fig. 3.2: IT is a major contributor to exports) and builds skills; developed countries oppose it because jobs move from their workers to low-wage countries. Exercise 11: low wage rates and availability of skilled manpower. The Recap adds that outsourcing is emerging as a major activity in industrial and service sectors.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, what made India a destination for global outsourcing?
options: Low wage rates and available skilled manpower
High import tariffs and strict licensing
A ban on foreign companies in services
Free electricity for IT companies
quiz.why: NCERT: the low wage rates and availability of skilled manpower in India have made it a destination for global outsourcing.

cards.q: Define outsourcing (NCERT).
cards.a: A company hiring regular service from external sources, mostly from other countries, which was previously provided internally.

cards.q: Name five services outsourced to India.
cards.a: BPOs/call centres, record keeping, accountancy, banking services, music recording, film editing, book transcription, clinical advice, teaching.

cards.q: What two advantages make India a favourite outsourcing destination (Exercise 11)?
cards.a: Low wage rates and availability of skilled manpower.

cards.q: According to NCERT's Recap, globalisation is the outcome of which policies?
cards.a: Liberalisation and privatisation.

reels.title: Concept: FDI vs FII, and India goes global

scenes.heading: Two kinds of foreign investment

left.title: FDI: foreign direct investment
items: Builds or buys into a business
Long-term, with a say in management
e.g. Hyundai's car plant near Chennai

right.title: FII: foreign institutional investment
items: Buys shares and bonds in markets
Can move in and out quickly
e.g. a foreign pension fund buying Indian shares

scenes.say: NCERT names both kinds of foreign investment but doesn't define them, so here's the difference, beyond the book. Foreign direct investment, F D I, means building or buying into a business for the long term, with a say in management, like Hyundai's car plant near Chennai. Foreign institutional investment, F I I, means buying shares and bonds in financial markets. It can move in and out quickly, like a foreign pension fund buying Indian shares. Think of buying a house and moving in, versus renting a room you can leave at a month's notice.

scenes.heading: Why the difference matters

items.text: FDI brings factories, jobs and technology, and stays
FII is 'hot money': quick to leave in a crisis

scenes.say: Why it matters: F D I brings factories, jobs and technology, and tends to stay. F I I money, sometimes called hot money, can leave quickly when there's trouble, which can shake the stock market and the rupee.

scenes.heading: Box 3.2: Indian companies go global

items.text: ONGC Videsh: projects in 16 countries
Tata Steel (founded 1907): operations in 26 countries, sells in 50
HCL Technologies: offices in 31 countries
Dr Reddy's: plants and research centres worldwide

scenes.say: Globalisation runs both ways. NCERT's Box 3.2 shows Indian companies expanding abroad. O N G C Videsh, a subsidiary of the public sector Oil and Natural Gas Corporation, has projects in 16 countries. Tata Steel, founded in 1907, operates in 26 countries and sells in 50, employing nearly 50,000 people abroad. H C L Technologies has offices in 31 countries. And Dr Reddy's grew from a small supplier into a company with plants and research centres around the world. These figures are NCERT's snapshot, from rediff dot com in 2014.

reels.beyond: Since 2014, India's regulator SEBI has used the term Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) in place of FII. A foreign stake of 10% or more in a company is generally counted as FDI, and smaller stakes as portfolio investment.
reels.examAngle: FDI vs FII is a frequent RBI Grade B question. Give long-term vs short-term, control vs no control, and an example of each.

quiz.q: A foreign company setting up its own manufacturing plant in India is an example of:
options: Foreign direct investment (FDI)
Foreign institutional investment (FII)
A quantitative restriction
Disinvestment
quiz.why: Building or buying into a business for the long term, with management control, is FDI. FII is buying shares and bonds in financial markets.

cards.q: FDI vs FII (beyond NCERT)?
cards.a: FDI: long-term investment in a business with a say in management (e.g. a factory). FII: buying shares and bonds in financial markets, can exit quickly.

cards.q: Give two examples from NCERT's Box 3.2 of Indian companies abroad.
cards.a: ONGC Videsh (projects in 16 countries); Tata Steel (26 countries, sells in 50); HCL (offices in 31 countries); Dr Reddy's.

reels.title: The WTO and its critics

scenes.heading: From GATT to WTO

events.text: GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) set up with 23 countries
World Trade Organisation (WTO) founded as its successor

scenes.say: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, or G A T T, was set up in 1948 with 23 countries, to administer multilateral trade agreements with equal opportunities for all countries. In 1995, the World Trade Organisation, the W T O, was founded as its successor. NCERT writes it as the General Agreement on Trade and Tariff; the official name is the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, so use that in exams.

scenes.heading: What the WTO aims for

items.text: A rule-based trading regime: no arbitrary trade restrictions
Enlarge production and trade of services
Optimum use of world resources; protect the environment
Remove tariff and non-tariff barriers, for goods and services

scenes.say: The W T O aims for a rule-based trading regime, where nations can't place arbitrary restrictions on trade. It also aims to enlarge production and trade of services, ensure optimum use of world resources and protect the environment. Its agreements cover goods and services, and promote both bilateral and multilateral trade by removing tariff and non-tariff barriers.

scenes.heading: Two pairs of terms

left.title: Bilateral vs multilateral
items: Bilateral: trade deal between two countries
Multilateral: among many countries at once

right.title: Tariff vs non-tariff barrier
items: Tariff: a tax on imports
Non-tariff: any other obstacle, e.g. quotas, strict standards

scenes.say: Exercise 6 asks you to distinguish these, so here are the definitions, beyond the book. Bilateral trade is between two countries; multilateral trade involves many countries at once. A tariff barrier is a tax on imports. A non-tariff barrier is any other obstacle, like quotas or very strict product standards.

scenes.heading: India and the WTO

left.title: India's role
items: Pushes for fair rules for developing countries
Removed QRs and cut tariffs as committed

right.title: Critics ask
items: Most trade is among developed nations
Developed countries file complaints over farm subsidies
Developing countries open up but get no access

scenes.say: As an important member, India has pushed for fair global rules and the interests of developing countries, and kept its commitments by removing quantitative restrictions and reducing tariffs. But some scholars question its value. Most international trade happens among developed nations. While developed countries file complaints over agricultural subsidies, developing countries feel cheated: forced to open their markets, without access to developed markets.

reels.beyond: The WTO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. Its top decision-making body is the Ministerial Conference, which meets about every two years. GATT was signed by 23 countries in 1947 and came into force on 1 January 1948. NCERT gives 1948; if an MCQ offers only 1947, that is the signing year.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 2: membership gives a rule-based trading regime where nations can't place arbitrary restrictions, greater market access as tariff and non-tariff barriers fall, and a voice in framing global rules; India uses it to advocate the interests of developing countries. Exercise 6(ii) bilateral vs multilateral and 6(iii) tariff vs non-tariff barriers. Dates: GATT 1948 (23 countries), WTO 1995. NCERT spells GATT as 'General Agreement on Trade and Tariff'; the official name is 'General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade'.

quiz.q: Which is correct about GATT and the WTO, according to NCERT?
options: GATT was set up in 1948 with 23 countries; the WTO replaced it in 1995
GATT was set up in 1948 with 23 countries; the WTO replaced it in 1991
GATT was set up in 1995 with 23 countries; the WTO replaced it in 2001
GATT was set up in 1948 with 123 countries; the WTO replaced it in 1995
quiz.why: NCERT: GATT was established in 1948 with 23 countries; the WTO was founded in 1995 as its successor.

cards.q: When were GATT and the WTO set up?
cards.a: GATT: 1948, with 23 countries. WTO: 1995, as GATT's successor.

cards.q: What are the WTO's aims (NCERT)?
cards.a: A rule-based trading regime without arbitrary restrictions; enlarge production and trade of services; optimum use of world resources; protect the environment.

cards.q: Bilateral vs multilateral trade; tariff vs non-tariff barrier?
cards.a: Bilateral: two countries; multilateral: many. Tariff: a tax on imports; non-tariff: other obstacles such as quotas or strict standards.

reels.title: Growth after 1991: the scorecard

scenes.label: GDP growth, 1980–91
scenes.say: Three decades on, how did the economy do? Growth is measured by G D P, gross domestic product: the total value of the final goods and services a country produces in a year. NCERT's Table 3.1 shows G D P growth rising from 5.6 percent in 1980 to 91, to 9.4 percent in 2021-22.

scenes.heading: Overall GDP growth by period (%)
scenes.say: Here's the whole row from Table 3.1. Overall G D P grew 5.6 percent a year in 1980 to 91, then 6.4 in 1992 to 2001, 7.8 in 2002 to 07, and 8.2 in 2007 to 12. It dipped to 5.6 in 2012-13, recovered to 6.6 in 2013-14, and reached 9.4 in 2021-22.

scenes.heading: Average growth by sector, 1980–91 (%)
scenes.say: Before the reforms, from 1980 to 91, industry grew 7.1 percent a year, services 6.7 percent, and agriculture 3.6 percent.

scenes.heading: Average growth by sector, 2007–12 (%)
scenes.say: By 2007 to 12, services led at 10 percent, industry grew 7.4 percent, and agriculture just 3.2 percent. NCERT's reading: agriculture's growth declined, industry fluctuated, and services rose, so G D P growth is mainly driven by the service sector; the Recap puts it as agriculture and industry growth going down. 2012-13 saw a setback across sectors. One caution: NCERT says services grew faster than overall G D P during 2007 to 2022, yet in the table's 2021-22 column services, at 9.2, are just below the total of 9.4.

scenes.heading: GDP and GVA, in plain words

items.text: GDP: total value of final goods and services produced in the country in a year
Gross value added (GVA): the value each producer adds, output minus inputs used up
Baker buys flour for ₹60, sells bread for ₹100: value added ₹40

scenes.say: Beyond the book, two terms. G D P is the total value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year. G V A, gross value added, measures the value each producer adds: a baker who buys flour for 60 rupees and sells bread for 100 adds 40. India reports growth sector by sector as G V A.

scenes.heading: GDP vs GVA

items.text: 2021-22 sector figures are GVA: agriculture 4.8, industry 12.7, services 9.2 (%)
NCERT: GVA = GDP + subsidies on production − indirect taxes

scenes.say: One note on the table: its 2021-22 sector figures, agriculture 4.8, industry 12.7 and services 9.2 percent, are gross value added, or G V A, not G D P. NCERT explains that G V A is estimated from G D P by adding subsidies on production and subtracting indirect taxes. So the two are close, but not the same.

reels.beyond: India switched to the GVA-based way of reporting sector growth in 2015, with 2011-12 as the base year. In February 2026 the base year was revised to 2022-23, so newer data will not match NCERT’s table exactly.
reels.examAngle: Know the headline numbers (5.6% in 1980-91, 9.4% in 2021-22) and the trend: services drive growth. Exercise 13 asks why services grew fast; link it to IT, outsourcing and globalisation.

quiz.q: According to NCERT's Table 3.1, which sector drove India's GDP growth in the reform period?
options: Services
Agriculture
Mining
Handicrafts
quiz.why: NCERT: agriculture's growth declined, industry fluctuated and services rose, indicating GDP growth is mainly driven by the service sector.

cards.q: GDP growth before and after reforms (NCERT Table 3.1)?
How does NCERT say GVA is estimated from GDP?
cards.a: By adding subsidies on production and subtracting indirect taxes.

cards.q: What trend in sector growth does NCERT see after 1991?
cards.a: Agriculture's growth declined, industry fluctuated, services rose, so GDP growth is mainly driven by services.

cards.q: GDP vs GVA in one line?
cards.a: GDP: value of all final goods and services produced in a year. GVA: value added by producers (output minus inputs). NCERT: GVA = GDP + subsidies on production − indirect taxes.

cards.q: Overall GDP growth by period (NCERT Table 3.1)?

reels.title: The gains: investment, reserves, exports

scenes.label: forex reserves, 1990-91
scenes.say: Remember the reserves that couldn't last two weeks? NCERT says foreign exchange reserves rose from about 6 billion dollars in 1990-91 to about 646 billion dollars in 2023-24. India is now one of the largest holders of foreign exchange reserves in the world.

scenes.label: foreign investment (FDI + FII), 1990-91
scenes.say: Opening up led to a rapid rise in foreign investment. Foreign investment, which includes foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investment, rose from about 100 million dollars in 1990-91 to 23 billion dollars in 2022-23.

scenes.heading: India the exporter

items.text: Auto parts
Pharmaceutical goods
Engineering goods
IT software
Textiles

scenes.say: Since 1991, India has become a successful exporter of auto parts, pharmaceutical goods, engineering goods, I T software and textiles. And NCERT adds that rising prices have also been kept under control.

reels.beyond: RBI publishes forex reserve figures every week in its Weekly Statistical Supplement. Reserves are made up of foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and India's reserve position with the IMF.
reels.examAngle: Classic 'then vs now' numbers: forex reserves $6 billion to $646 billion; foreign investment $100 million to $23 billion. These are the reform's clearest successes.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, India's foreign exchange reserves rose from about $6 billion in 1990-91 to about:
options: $646 billion in 2023-24
$64 billion in 2023-24
$23 billion in 2022-23
$6,460 billion in 2023-24
quiz.why: NCERT: from about US $6 billion in 1990-91 to about US $646 billion in 2023-24. ($23 billion is the foreign investment figure for 2022-23.)

cards.q: Forex reserves before and after reforms (NCERT)?
cards.a: About $6 billion in 1990-91 to about $646 billion in 2023-24.

cards.q: Foreign investment (FDI + FII) before and after reforms (NCERT)?
cards.a: About $100 million in 1990-91 to $23 billion in 2022-23.

cards.q: Name five exports India became successful in after 1991.
cards.a: Auto parts, pharmaceutical goods, engineering goods, IT software and textiles.

reels.title: Why farmers lost out

scenes.heading: The critique of reforms

items.text: Employment
Agriculture
Industry
Infrastructure
Fiscal management

scenes.say: The reforms have been widely criticised for failing to address basic problems in employment, agriculture, industry, infrastructure and fiscal management. NCERT adds that the evidence so far shows this criticism is not completely true, and asks what you think. Scholars also point out that reform-led growth hasn't generated enough jobs. Let's start with agriculture, where NCERT says the reforms haven't benefited farmers and growth has been decelerating.

scenes.heading: What hurt agriculture

items.text: Public investment fell: irrigation, power, roads, market links, research
Partial removal of fertiliser subsidy raised costs for small farmers
Lower import duties, low minimum support prices (MSP) and no QRs: foreign competition
Shift to export cash crops pushed up food grain prices

scenes.say: Since 1991, public investment in farm infrastructure, like irrigation, power, roads, market linkages, and research and extension, has fallen. Partial removal of the fertiliser subsidy raised costs, hurting small and marginal farmers. Lower import duties, low minimum support prices, or M S P, the price at which the government promises to buy certain crops, and lifting quantitative restrictions exposed farmers to international competition. And export-oriented policies shifted farming from food grains to cash crops, putting pressure on food grain prices.

scenes.heading: Mahadeva's story (NCERT)
steps: Groundnut farmer in drought-prone Anantpur, Andhra Pradesh
Spent ₹10,000; earned ₹14,000 (2 quintals × ₹7,000)
No major irrigation; crop disease; less research and extension
Lower subsidy raises his costs
Cheap imported edible oils flood the market
He can't sell at a price that covers his cost
scenes.say: NCERT tells the story of Mahadeva, a groundnut farmer in drought-prone Anantpur, Andhra Pradesh. He used to spend 10,000 rupees on his half-acre plot and earn 14,000: two quintals at 7,000 rupees each. After the reforms, the government didn't undertake any major irrigation project. His groundnut faced crop disease, while research and extension work went down. Lower subsidies raised his costs. Then cheap imported edible oils flooded local markets after import restrictions were removed. Mahadeva couldn't sell his groundnut at a price that covered his cost.

reels.beyond: Minimum support price (MSP) is the price at which the government promises to buy certain crops from farmers. It is announced each season on the advice of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP).
reels.examAngle: Exercise 14: why was agriculture adversely affected by reforms? List the four reasons: falling public investment, fertiliser subsidy cuts, import liberalisation with low MSP, and the shift to cash crops.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, which of these hurt Indian agriculture after the reforms?
options: Fall in public investment in farm infrastructure
A big rise in fertiliser subsidies
Higher import duties on farm products
New quantitative restrictions on imports
quiz.why: NCERT: public investment in agricultural infrastructure fell; fertiliser subsidy was partially removed; import duties were reduced and QRs lifted.

cards.q: Give four reasons agriculture suffered after the reforms (Exercise 14).
cards.a: Falling public investment in infrastructure; partial removal of fertiliser subsidy; lower import duties, low MSP and removal of QRs; shift to export cash crops pressuring food grain prices.

cards.q: What does the Mahadeva case in NCERT show?
cards.a: A groundnut farmer in Anantpur lost out: no irrigation, less research, lower subsidy, and cheap imported edible oils meant he couldn't cover his costs.

reels.title: Industry's slowdown and non-tariff barriers

scenes.heading: Why industry slowed

items.text: Cheaper imports replace demand for Indian goods
Domestic makers face import competition
Too little investment in infrastructure like power

scenes.say: Industrial growth also slowed, NCERT says, because demand for industrial products fell. Cheaper imports replaced demand for domestic goods, so Indian manufacturers faced competition from imports. And infrastructure, including power supply, stayed inadequate for lack of investment.

scenes.heading: A one-way street?

items.text: Developing countries must open up to goods and capital from rich countries
Local industries and jobs suffer

scenes.say: In a globalised world, developing countries are compelled to open up to a greater flow of goods and capital from developed countries, making their industries vulnerable to imports. So globalisation is often seen as creating conditions that hurt local industries and jobs in developing countries.

scenes.heading: Non-tariff barriers: NCERT's example

left.title: India
items: Removed all quota restrictions on its textile and clothing exports

right.title: USA
items: Kept quotas on textile imports from India and China

scenes.say: And India still lacks access to developed countries' markets because of high non-tariff barriers. NCERT's example: although India removed all quota restrictions on exports of textiles and clothing, the U S A did not remove its quota restrictions on textile imports from India and China.

reels.beyond: Many non-tariff barriers today take the form of strict product standards. Examples are food safety and pesticide limits, and technical rules on electronics. NCERT's textile example is dated: textile quotas between WTO members ended on 1 January 2005, when the Agreement on Textiles and Clothing expired. Use NCERT's example for NCERT questions.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 15: why did industry perform poorly? Cheaper imports, inadequate infrastructure investment, and developed countries' non-tariff barriers (the USA's textile quota example).

quiz.q: What example does NCERT give of a non-tariff barrier faced by India?
options: The USA keeping quotas on textile imports from India and China
India cutting its own export duties on cotton textiles and clothing
The WTO lowering its tariffs on Indian textiles and readymade garments
Britain putting a special tax on software exports coming from India
quiz.why: NCERT: although India removed quota restrictions on textile and clothing exports, the USA did not remove its quota restriction on textile imports from India and China.

cards.q: Why did industrial growth slow after the reforms (NCERT)?
cards.a: Falling demand due to cheaper imports, inadequate infrastructure investment (e.g. power), and competition from imports.

cards.q: NCERT's example of a non-tariff barrier?
cards.a: The USA kept quota restrictions on textile imports from India and China, even after India removed its textile quotas.

reels.title: Disinvestment and fiscal policy: the critique

scenes.heading: Disinvestment targets

events.text: Target ₹2,500 crore; NCERT: ₹3,040 crore mobilised, more than the target

scenes.say: Every year, the government sets a disinvestment target. In 1991-92, it aimed to raise 2,500 crore rupees through disinvestment, and NCERT says it mobilised 3,040 crore rupees, more than the target. In 2022-23, it raised about 46,000 crore rupees.

scenes.heading: The critics

items.text: PSE assets undervalued and sold to the private sector
A substantial loss to the government
Proceeds used to fill revenue gaps, not to build PSEs or social infrastructure

scenes.say: Critics say the assets of public sector enterprises were undervalued and sold to the private sector, a substantial loss to the government. And the money raised was used to make up for shortfalls in government revenue, rather than to develop the enterprises or build social infrastructure.

scenes.heading: Reforms and fiscal policy

items.text: Limits on public spending, especially in social sectors
Tax cuts didn't raise revenue as hoped
Lower tariffs meant less customs revenue
Tax incentives for foreign investors cut revenue further

scenes.say: Reforms also limited growth in public expenditure, especially in social sectors. Tax cuts meant to raise revenue and curb evasion didn't increase tax revenue. Lower tariffs reduced revenue from customs duties, and tax incentives to attract foreign investors reduced it further. NCERT says this hurt developmental and welfare spending.

reels.beyond: NCERT's line 'mobilise ₹3,040 crore more than the target' can be misread as ₹3,040 crore over the target; the 1991-92 receipts were about ₹3,040 crore in total. Disinvestment targets were often missed. Since the 2024-25 Interim Budget, the Budget no longer gives a separate disinvestment target; disinvestment and asset monetisation are counted together as ‘miscellaneous capital receipts’ (₹80,000 crore budgeted for 2026-27).
reels.examAngle: Exercise 9 (should profit-making PSUs be privatised?): either view if argued. For: financial discipline, modernisation, private capital and management, FDI. Against: assets undervalued, proceeds used to fill revenue gaps; and NCERT’s Box 3.1 notes the government decided to keep profitable PSEs public and let them grow globally. Exercise 16 (reforms and social justice): use the critics’ points here, including squeezed welfare spending.

quiz.q: According to NCERT's critics, how were disinvestment proceeds mostly used?
options: To offset the shortage of government revenue
To build new public sector enterprises
To expand social infrastructure across India
To raise subsidies for small farmers
quiz.why: NCERT: critics point out that disinvestment proceeds were used to offset the shortage of government revenues rather than to develop PSEs and social infrastructure.

cards.q: Disinvestment: 1991-92 target and result, and 2022-23 (NCERT)?
cards.a: 1991-92: target ₹2,500 crore, ₹3,040 crore mobilised, more than the target; 2022-23: about ₹46,000 crore.

cards.q: Two criticisms of disinvestment (NCERT)?
cards.a: PSE assets were undervalued and sold (a loss to the government); proceeds offset revenue shortages instead of developing PSEs or social infrastructure.

cards.q: How did reforms hurt government revenue (NCERT)?
cards.a: Tax cuts didn't raise revenue, lower tariffs cut customs revenue, and tax incentives to foreign investors reduced it further, so welfare spending suffered.

reels.title: The verdict on LPG, and Siricilla

scenes.heading: Box 3.3: the Siricilla tragedy
steps: Power reforms end subsidised electricity; tariffs rise steeply
Powerloom weavers' wages are tied to cloth output
Power cuts mean wage cuts
Crisis: 50 powerloom workers die by suicide in Siricilla
scenes.say: Box 3.3 shows reforms' human cost. Power sector reforms in many states ended subsidised electricity and raised tariffs steeply. Powerloom workers in Andhra Pradesh are paid by the cloth they produce, so a power cut means a wage cut. A crisis followed, and 50 powerloom workers committed suicide in the small town of Siricilla.

scenes.heading: Globalisation: opportunity or threat?

left.title: Opportunity
items: Access to global markets
High technology
Indian firms become global players

right.title: Threat
items: Developed countries expand their markets
Welfare and identity of poor countries compromised
Wider disparities among nations and people

scenes.say: NCERT's conclusion: globalisation through liberalisation and privatisation has had positive and negative results. Some see an opportunity: greater access to global markets, high technology, and Indian firms becoming global players. Critics see a strategy of developed countries to expand their markets, which has compromised the welfare and identity of poor countries and widened disparities among nations and people.

scenes.heading: The Indian critique

items.text: The 1991 crisis came from deep-rooted inequalities
The externally advised reform package made inequality worse
Growth concentrated in services: telecom, IT, finance, entertainment, travel and hospitality, real estate, trade
Not in agriculture and industry, which support millions

scenes.say: In India, some studies say the early 1990s crisis grew out of deep-rooted inequalities, and the externally advised reform package made them worse. Growth increased the income and quality of consumption of only high-income groups, and was concentrated in services like telecommunication, information technology, finance, entertainment, travel and hospitality, real estate and trade, rather than in agriculture and industry, which give livelihoods to millions.

reels.beyond: Siricilla, in NCERT's Andhra Pradesh, has been in Telangana since the state was formed in 2014.
reels.examAngle: Exercise 16 (reforms, social justice and welfare): balance the gains (growth, reserves, investment, exports) against the critique (jobs, agriculture, inequality, the Siricilla example). A must-practise descriptive question for ESI.

quiz.q: In NCERT's Box 3.3, what triggered the crisis among Siricilla's powerloom workers?
options: An end to subsidised electricity and a steep rise in power tariffs
A sudden government ban on all textile exports from India to the West
A collapse in the price of imported cotton yarn that flooded local markets
A new, much higher GST rate on handloom and powerloom cloth sold in India
quiz.why: NCERT: power sector reforms ended subsidised electricity and raised power tariffs steeply; since weavers' wages were linked to output, power cuts meant wage cuts.

cards.q: What was the Siricilla tragedy (Box 3.3)?
cards.a: Power reforms ended subsidised electricity and raised tariffs; powerloom weavers' output-linked wages fell; 50 powerloom workers committed suicide in Siricilla, Andhra Pradesh.

cards.q: In which sectors does NCERT say post-reform growth was concentrated?
cards.a: Services such as telecom, IT, finance, entertainment, travel and hospitality, real estate and trade, not agriculture and industry.
